catalog_quote: [p.1, abstract] Kunama has been reported by different scholars as having two or three tones, downstep (or not), contrastive length of both consonants and vowels, and lexical stress. ... we present phonological and phonetic evidence for the existence of three level tones ... No evidence for lexical stress is found. [pp.2-3] ... Tucker and Bryan [1966] ... observe that "[t]one and stress appear to be significant, both lexically and grammatically." [1966: 337]. ... [Thompson] was of the opinion that there was a correlation between vowel length and stress [1983: 284]. ... Elsewhere stress is reported as usually occurring on syllables preceding geminates [1983: 283]. These statements would appear to suggest an accentual assignment that was sensitive to syllable weight. ... Bender also comes out in support of Thompson's interpretation of many aspects of prosodic prominence in Kunama as involv…

tone_statements.citation: Ashkaba, John Abraha & Richard J. Hayward. 1999. Kunama. (Illustrations of the IPA.) Journal of the International Phonetic Association 29(2): 179-185. doi:10.1017/S0025100300006551
tone_statements.quote: The Kunama are a people of western Eritrea. Kunama (/ku 1 naa 23 ma 2 /) is their selfname, and they call their language /ku 1 naa 23 ma 1 au 23 ra 2 / or /ki 1 naa 23 ma 1 ɲeel 23 a 2 / but this is usually referred to by Western scholars simply as ‘Kunama’. ... It comprises seven lects (John Abraha Ashkaba 1999), the most widely known of which are Barka (/ba 2 ka 2 /) and Marda (/mar 2 da 32 /). The present work is based on the latter, though the differences between these two lects is not very great.

Second-hand: Anteneh Getachew 2018 (AAU PhD, p. 165, sec. 6.1 'Tone Inventory') reports 'Banti and Nikodimos (1994) have proposed high, low and a downstep', i.e. a two-level-plus-downstep analysis, against the three-level (H, M, L) analyses of Tucker & Bryan 1966, Connell et al. 2000 and Getachew 2018; Getachew (p. 33) also singles it out as the only unpublished Kunama study that is not an AAU BA/MA thesis. Ashkaba & Hayward 1999 list it among 'more recent studies' of the language.
